GPT-Live has pushed aside the older turn-based Advanced Voice to become the default. You start it by tapping the waveform-shaped ChatGPT Voice icon at the far right of the input box. The first time, you'll be asked for microphone permission.

blocks.cap: The ChatGPT Voice settings screen.

blocks.x: Entering voice mode brings up an orb on screen that reacts to you. You just talk as usual. The settings icon at the top right lets you pick the model's intelligence level from Instant, Medium, or High. GPT-Live-1 mini doesn't have this setting, so it requires a paid plan. ChatGPT Voice keeps running even if you switch to another app or lock your device.

GPT-Live still doesn't support screen sharing or video sharing, though. You can go back to the older voice model by choosing a different model under Voice in settings. From the same place, you can change the voice and language, or set ChatGPT Voice to open by default when you launch the app.

blocks.cap: The ChatGPT app icon on an iPhone home screen.

blocks.x: The author, who prefers typing, wasn't especially interested in the new voice mode at first—not until having a few long conversations with it. What stood out wasn't how smart it was, but how quickly it became easy to forget you were talking to an AI. It doesn't interrupt you, and you don't have to wait awkwardly for it to finish. When a question runs long, it almost feels like it senses what you're about to say next.

Because it responds so quickly, it's also usable for real-time interpretation. Scrolling down during a conversation brings up a transcript of what was said. For questions better served visually, it builds and displays an interactive widget alongside its spoken answer.

The default intelligence level is Instant. It favors fast responses while still handling everyday questions without trouble, and hands off searches or deep reasoning to a stronger model behind the scenes without breaking the conversation. For anyone who deals with complex topics often, Medium and High take a beat or two longer to think, but that delay doesn't disrupt the flow of conversation.

blocks.cap: Image courtesy of Square Enix.

blocks.x: Keeping sketches and drafts may be the only proof left that a human made something.
The controversy now facing Square Enix, the Japanese publisher behind Final Fantasy and Kingdom Hearts, is the kind that anyone who makes a living creating things should pay attention to.

As a sister outlet reported, the cover art for the Kingdom Hearts collection, coming to the Switch 2 and other platforms, drew suspicion of being AI-generated within hours of its reveal. The evidence stands out: Donald Duck has three fingers on one hand and four on the other. The watch's details don't line up, the keychains are inconsistent in size, and the whole thing looks sloppy.
Square Enix said it wasn't AI. According to its statement, the image was made by the development team without generative tools, and the errors were human mistakes.

That may well be true. The problem is that no one outside the studio has any way to verify it. Even after the cover was revised three times, fixing some errors while leaving others, the doubt remained. The real story is that uncertainty, and it's bigger than one publisher's cover art problem.
“A human made this” is no longer a sentence that companies or freelancers get to say and simply be believed. It has to be shown. A long-held assumption has flipped.

For decades, people assumed their own work was theirs by default. Why would anyone think otherwise? Now it's the reverse. If a piece of work has even a hint of so-called AI tells, the burden of explanation falls on the person who made it, and “trust me” no longer works.

The fortunate part is that keeping a record of process was already a good habit before any of this. Sketches, rough cuts, contact sheets, and early drafts have always had value—proof of range and skill that the finished piece alone can't show, and promotional material to use later. One reason people respond so well to this kind of content on social media is that it offers clues and texture they can't get anywhere else.

It also benefits the person doing the work. Writing down why a decision was made, whether as a caption or just a private note to yourself, sharpens the decision itself. Half of a sketchbook lives in writing that never gets shared. This isn't new advice. What's new is the size of what's at stake.

Keeping process records used to be a bonus for whenever there was spare time and energy. By the late 2020s, it has become close to essential for any work that could be mistaken for machine-made. Files with live layers, time-stamped drafts, reference boards, even screen recordings of work taking shape—all of it may be needed someday to prove you made it.

So don't throw away rough drafts, keep version history turned on, screen-record when the software allows it, and hold on to files even when it seems you'll never need them again. Suspicion of being machine-made costs clients, work, and reputation, even when it isn't true.
The Gnomon Workshop released Design Mechs in VR Using Substance 3D Modeler. It's a free guide to a VR sculpting workflow, recorded by WB Games concept artist Andre-Lang Huynh.
It's a 30-minute video course covering Substance 3D Modeler and KeyShot.

In the course, Huynh shows his entire workflow for designing and sculpting a mech from scratch using Adobe's VR sculpting software, Substance 3D Modeler. He starts from simple geometric shapes, locking down proportion and silhouette first, then builds up complexity with secondary and tertiary forms like joints and armor plating, plus color and surface detail.
The Substance 3D Modeler features covered include primitives, sculpting brushes, booleans, layers, materials, stamps, symmetry, angle snapping, and reusable kitbash elements.

Once sculpting is done, he moves into KeyShot to apply materials, set up simple lighting, and produce presentation renders. The project files that come with the workshop include the finished Substance 3D Modeler scene.
Andre-Lang Huynh is an advanced concept artist at WB Games Montréal. He designed characters, props, and vehicles on Gotham Knights, including the Batmobile and the Batcycle.

Design Mechs in VR Using Substance 3D Modeler is available through a subscription to The Gnomon Workshop, which includes more than 300 tutorials. The subscription costs $57 a month or $499 a year, with a free trial available.
